articles.title: The questions Jensen Huang and Nvidia will still have to answer about Megaspeed | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The central question for investigators is what Nvidia knew about where those chips ended up and whether Huang's affair with a Megaspeed executive gave the company reason to doubt Megaspeed's assurances.
articles.body_text: Jensen Huang’s return as CEO to Nvidia hasn’t eased the scrutiny the company faces. The chipmaker still needs to address multiple inquiries into allegations that its advanced GPUs were smuggled into China by a customer, the Singapore-based data center operator Megaspeed, in violation of U.S. export rules designed to slow China’s development of frontier AI models. The central question for investigators is what Nvidia knew about where those chips ended up and whether Huang’s affair with a Megaspeed executive gave the company reason to doubt Megaspeed’s assurances. Huang’s return doesn’t settle that. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche has suggested Nvidia isn’t a target of an investigation, but California’s attorney general and Congress are pressing ahead, and the Securities and Exchange Commission is reportedly investigating, too. The U.S. government opened an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 and requested information from Nvidia about its billions of dollars in sales to the company, concerned that some of the chips Megaspeed bought for data center projects in Malaysia were in fact being diverted to China. Singapore also began investigating similar allegations in 2025. Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing. Diversion of this kind would be a fairly routine issue for a company like Nvidia, whose in-demand chips are the targets of smugglers and resellers. When it comes to compliance and liability for export-control violations, Nvidia and other chip sellers need assurances that the end users of their chips are obeying the rules. However, they also cannot ignore other information that might call the reliability of those assurances into question, export-control attorneys told TechCrunch. And that’s why Jensen Huang’s affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang was such a problem for Nvidia, likely even more so than her alleged role as a source for Chinese intelligence agencies. If Nvidia personnel, from lower-level employees up to the CEO, had reason to believe that statements from Megaspeed weren’t reliable, the attorneys said, that would increase the company’s legal risk. “Government investigators likely would want to know, notwithstanding whatever formal assurances were exchanged between the parties, what anyone at Nvidia actually knew about the end use and end users of the chips,” Dan Fisher-Owens, an attorney at the firm Berliner Corcoran & Rowe, told TechCrunch last week. The concern Nvidia’s board faced when it decided to oust Huang is that he knew more about what Megaspeed was doing with Nvidia’s products than was reflected in any of the compliance statements. The Wall Street Journal reported that Alice Huang and her husband, Kang Wei, were part of a network of businesses that funneled chips to a company in Shanghai. Kang also reportedly introduced his wife to Jensen Huang, whom he had known for a decade. On Monday, the U.S. government added Megaspeed and its affiliates to a list of companies restricted from U.S. trade due to national security concerns. The U.S. also issued new rules last week barring large data centers that purchase U.S. chips from serving customers in China and other nations seen as problematic by the U.S. government. Nvidia, meanwhile, said it would stop selling licensed chips to China and laid out plans to hire its first compliance officer and create a new board committee focused on export controls. Nvidia’s board said it reinstated Huang on Monday after receiving “input from senior levels of the United States government” that left it confident his return posed no national security risk. President Donald Trump later said he called into the meeting to give them that assurance. In a news conference Tuesday, Blanche said that Nvidia was “a good corporate citizen” and suggested it is not the target of an investigation, but Blanche declined to answer questions about the government’s investigation into Megaspeed, which the Justice Department said was ongoing as recently as last week. “When you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don’t know what you’re talking about,” Blanche said. Other authorities may be more demanding. Nvidia faces investigations by California Attorney General Rob Bonta and, reportedly , the SEC, both tied to its corporate disclosures. While many details of the investigation still aren’t known, short sellers complained about the company’s decision to stop breaking out its exports to Singapore in financial filings after journalists raised concerns about chip diversion.

articles.title: Yale's Sonnenfeld: Nvidia is a 'detriment' to US industrial might — not a champion | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Yale's Jeffrey Sonnenfeld warns that what the market cheered Monday, Jensen Huang's White House–backed return as Nvidia's CEO and board member, could prove a giant mistake, exposing the directors to "historic" personal liability from a growing pile of lawsuits and raising the question of whether the country is celebrating a company that has helped put advanced chips in its adversaries' hands.
articles.body_text: Investors cheered Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia’s CEO on Monday, but renowned business academic Jeffrey Sonnenfeld of Yale thinks they’re celebrating a mistake. He sees a company that is largely responsible for putting sophisticated technology in the hands of the country’s adversaries, at a moment when the risks couldn’t be higher . Far from a champion of American industry, he says, Nvidia is “a detriment to U.S. global industrial might.” As evidence, Sonnenfeld points to research suggesting Nvidia’s most advanced chips have reached China despite U.S. export controls and to sinking shares of Anthropic, which he links to the realization that China’s seemingly miraculous open source AI models are, in a sense, copies of top U.S. labs’ work, even as Nvidia has insisted that smuggling is a “non-factor.” Indeed, Huang’s return was greeted with just as much enthusiasm in Asia, The Washington Post reported. “The king is back!” read one headline from China’s state-affiliated Star Market Daily. The reinstatement itself followed heavy pressure from Washington. Nvidia’s chairman had effectively ruled out Huang’s return just last week. Then, in a torrent of private weekend calls led by Vice President JD Vance, top administration officials leaned on the board to welcome Huang back, with President Trump calling the board directly to vouch for him. “ I made the deal ,” Trump told CNBC on Monday. Sonnenfeld says the directors who went along, and who returned Huang to the board even as it investigates whether foreign intelligence efforts targeted him, now face a “historic level of individual liability.” The legal deluge has already begun. As we noted a couple of weeks ago , a potential class-action lawsuit was filed almost immediately. Days later, a shareholder derivative suit followed. Filed on Nvidia’s behalf against the directors themselves, the suit alleges the board ignored red flags about Huang’s relationship with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang. The class action is very much aimed at making Nvidia and Huang compensate investors for their losses, while the derivative suit puts the directors’ own behavior on trial, with any recovery going to Nvidia. Three more suits followed on November 18, the day after Nvidia’s most recent earnings call; all five were filed in Northern California, where Nvidia is based. Huang and Nvidia are also juggling a Justice Department antitrust investigation, a reported SEC probe into Nvidia’s accounting, a possible FBI review, a California subpoena , an export-control case that landed partner Megaspeed on the U.S. trade blacklist on Monday, and congressional inquiries, including a Senate Banking hearing next week at which Huang has agreed to testify. Here’s more of what Sonnenfeld had to say, in a Q&A that’s been edited for length and clarity. So much has happened since we last talked . Huang was ousted, he’s come back. Do you think the board’s reliance on government assurances here is defensible or an abdication of its own duties? They failed to rely on experts. That’s one of the reasons this board is going to be sued and lose, and these directors are likely to face a historic level of individual liability. They have a very inadequate directors and officers liability policy . They have also just failed in their diligence. They hired the Wachtell [law] firm. The Wachtell firm barely got off the blocks to do an investigation. And then they have already reversed themselves, so they didn’t use the expertise needed. It’s wild that they also put Huang right back on the board of directors.

articles.title: Jensen Huang still thinks a succession plan creates unnecessary hierarchy | TechCrunch
articles.summary: It's a remarkable stance for a company that spent the last two weeks finding out what happens without its founder.
articles.body_text: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang kicked off his return to the chipmaker he co-founded by holding an all-hands meeting that covered remorse, therapy, and even the company’s code of conduct, according to accounts from multiple insiders who spoke to the media. The topic of succession planning also came up — a particularly sticky issue seen as a key risk at Nvidia. Huang reportedly told staff that Nvidia doesn’t require succession planning because of its unique business model, CNBC reported , citing an unnamed source who was present. Surprisingly, given the events of the last two weeks, Huang argued that a succession plan would create unnecessary hierarchy. Investors and analysts saw the issue differently earlier this month, when Huang resigned as CEO following his admission that he had extramarital affairs with at least two people, including one whom the U.S. government suspects of being a Chinese spy. Nvidia is a flat organization, unlike other large corporations that have a swath of C-suite executives and multiple layers of management. Huang sits at the top and says he has about 60 direct reports. Nvidia has just five executive officers running the show, including Huang. The other four are CFO Colette Kress, who was interim CEO for 12 days; Ajay Puri, who heads worldwide field operations; Debora Shoquist, executive vice president of operations; and Timothy Teter, executive vice president and general counsel, according to the company’s regulatory filings . Huang has previously defended the company’s structure in numerous interviews, including one in March with podcaster Lex Fridman. “When you’re designing a company, you should first think about what is it that you want the company to produce,” Huang said in the interview. “You know, I see a lot of companies’ organization charts, and they all look the same. Hamburger [company] organization charts, software organization charts, and car company organization charts. They all look the same. And it doesn’t make any sense to me. You know, the goal of company is to be the machinery, the mechanism, the system that produces the output. And that output is the product that we like to create.” Huang’s comments to staff, and his previous remarks on the topic of succession, may not be enough to assuage the board or shareholders over the long term, however. articles.summary: The Nvidia founder apologized to his staff on Tuesday and said he was grateful for a second chance to lead the company.
articles.body_text: After a whirlwind period during which Jensen Huang’s life fell apart and then came back together again, the Nvidia founder now wants his staff to know that he’s a changed man. Huang held Nvidia’s first all-hands meeting on Tuesday since his reinstatement on Monday. During that meeting, CNBC reported that Huang struck a “remorseful tone” and told the crowd “I hurt all of you.” The founder, whose extramarital affairs have been accused of jeopardizing everything from the stock market to U.S. national security, went on to describe how difficult the current moment is for him: “This is going to be the hardest company meeting I’ve ever done, and the second hardest meeting I have ever done,” Huang reportedly told staff . “The hardest meeting I’ve ever done was with my wife,” he added. The CEO admitted in the meeting that he had flouted Nvidia’s code of conduct , which he himself had largely devised. Huang emphasized that the code of conduct was still in effect, but that mitigating circumstances would matter a lot. As Wired reported Huang’s statement, it “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door.” Huang told staff that he’s in therapy and also said that he was grateful for a second chance at the company. The CEO is now walking a difficult tight rope between reasserting his authority over one of the world’s most powerful and influential companies, and conceding that he may have made some mistakes. He also tackled the difficult question of President Trump’s role in his restoration. The president reportedly called Nvidia’s board directly to lobby for Huang’s return, but in his talk, Huang downplayed Trump’s role Huang thanked the administration on Tuesday for “providing Nvidia with quick access to intelligence that he said helped the board determine that the national security risks the company faced in reinstating him were low,” The Wall Street Journal writes . Huang will likely need the administration’s support as he weathers an upcoming wave of congressional scrutiny from a newly Democrat-led government. The CEO is scheduled to appear for a public Senate Banking Committee hearing next week and, in the coming weeks, he will be called to appear for a number of different closed House hearings, including for the Intelligence Committee, the Foreign Affairs Committee, and the China Select Committee. articles.title: Even the best AI agents struggle with everyday life | TechCrunch
articles.summary: As millions embrace personal AI assistants, a new benchmark reveals that even the most advanced AI models struggle to complete everyday tasks reliably and safely without introducing potential new problems.
articles.body_text: AI companies have spent the last couple of months marketing personal AI agents as tools to take over the digital drudgery of human existence — and millions have been sold on the vision, handing over their shopping schedules, travel plans, and everyday responsibilities to AI assistants. But new research suggests that even the most advanced AI models struggle to reliably and safely navigate the messy details of people’s lives. According to ShellBench, a new benchmark for everyday agent work, even the most advanced models from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta failed more than a third of the time. Across all models tested, 15.7% of attempts failed at least one safety requirement, often leading to unintended consequences. ShellBench was developed in collaboration with researchers at The OpenClaw Foundation, Parsewave, Hugging Face, Red Hat, and UC Berkeley, drawing on more than 10 million anonymized, real-world AI agent interactions to see how agents perform on the everyday work people actually delegate to them. The research comes as personal AI assistants are finding new popularity among developers, with Meta, OpenAI, and Anthropic all fighting for a piece of the market with Muse, Dots , and Claude Duet , respectively. In October, Meta said more than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada had set up its personal AI agent, Muse, within six weeks of launch, with about a quarter using it daily. That number is expected to grow as Meta implants Muse directly into Instagram DMs . Despite growing popularity among consumers, we still have little evidence about how reliable AI personal assistant products actually are. ShellBench suggests that the unreliable nature of most everyday data sources still causes problems for many state-of-the-art systems. A successful agent should be able to navigate messy personal workspaces containing emails, calendar entries, spreadsheets, receipts, chat logs, outdated information, and phishing attempts, and figure out which information is relevant, what is private, and how to deliver the requested outcome without creating new problems. It seems many of today’s AI agents are still not up to the task. Not only did even the highest-performing agents frequently fail to meet the requirements of a task, but they also lacked consistency. When researchers ran each task three times under identical conditions, OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, the highest-scoring model, nailed all three attempts less than half the time. For autonomous assistants that are meant to run in the background without supervision, it’s a problem if users need to run an agent multiple times to get a result they trust. Additionally, about 10% of otherwise correct attempts failed at least one safety criterion. Across the models and harnesses tested, agents failed to, for example, adequately account for a child’s school pickup 79.5% of the time. When handling laptop custody records, agents failed a requirement to identify and withhold a sensitive bank upload token in 18.6% of attempts. In another task, agents recommended duplicate or incorrect invoice payments 40.3% of the time. The findings highlight a major issue for users adopting consumer personal AI assistants, namely that there’s always a risk that an agent can create more headaches in the course of trying to fulfill an otherwise ordinary request. While AI benchmarks have largely focused on coding, professional work, or testing on specific tasks, ShellBench is attempting to evaluate how models perform on multi-step personal tasks within different agent harnesses — the software that controls how a model accesses information, uses tools, and takes actions. While the researchers found model choice had a greater overall impact on performance than harness choice, among the more capable models, AI agent performance became more dependent on the harness.

articles.title: Maple raises $5.3M to build AI products that protect your data, even from itself | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The startup's encrypted AI architecture is designed to prevent even the company itself from accessing users' private data.
articles.body_text: “We wanted to build something that was not only encrypted but also could be proven, and that people could go look at the open-source code, and then they could look at what we call trusted execution environments,” explains Maple co-founder and CEO Mark Suman . “They can look at and verify the code that’s running on our servers, so they don’t really have to take our word for it.” “They can audit everything themselves and know how their data is being handled,” he adds. Instead of asking users to trust that Maple won’t misuse their personal data, it’s attempting to build a business where it can’t access that data in the first place. Like other AI apps on the market, Maple allows users to engage in a chat experience where they ask questions and get answers. Meanwhile, its newly launched desktop app, Maple Work , offers a more agentic experience where the AI can control your computer, work with your files and apps, and control your browser to get online tasks handled. With the company’s recently closed $5.3 million round, it’s moving on to its next product — a cloud-based agent that will be able to continue its work even if your computer isn’t on. This addition would make Maple more competitive with other popular consumer AI services, like Meta’s Muse , Instinct , and other AI agents that work over chat. The app offers a familiar interface for those used to AI chatbots, but under the hood it runs a variety of open models, including versions of DeepSeek , Kimi , GLM , Inkling from Thinking Machines, Google’s Gemma , and OpenAI’s GPT OSS . Users can pick and choose the models they want or, for a simpler experience, just toggle between a quick model and the more powerful one. The models themselves run inside a trusted execution environment (TEE) — meaning a server with hardware encryption on it — within a U.S.-based data center. (Maple also offers support for European customers through a partner that runs its server in Europe.) “We actually don’t have access to [the data] while it’s inside the TEE,” explains Suman. “The data gets encrypted first on your device using a unique password that’s only known by you, the user — we don’t have access to it. It then goes into this TEE, and it gets decrypted inside there. The AI does its thing, and then it re-encrypts it with your password and sends it back to you,” he continues. “So we provide an end-to-end experience that’s very easy for the user, but we actually don’t have access to the raw data as it’s in flight or even when it’s at rest,” he adds. This allows Maple to protect its users’ data, even from outsiders — like if hackers breached its system or the government came with a subpoena, for instance. All it could do would be to hand over an encrypted file. “We just simply don’t want access to it,” Suman says of customers’ data. “That’s not part of our business model. And we also don’t want it to be part of our threat model.” Next year, Maple plans to enter the enterprise market with pilot work, where it will offer its own version of zero data retention. (Maple doesn’t retain most of the customers’ data, but when it has to, that data is encrypted.) It’s now in the process of completing SOC 2 compliance and security audits to get ready for this expansion. The company declined to share its registered customer numbers but noted it’s seen 60x growth over the past three months, as people have been looking for ways to increase their security with AI.

articles.title: Amazon’s online car ‘dealership’ with Hyundai is now live
articles.summary: Amazon is now selling vehicles through its website for the first time. The company has a deal with Hyundai to feature dealer models in 48 cities in the US.
articles.body_text: Today, for the first time, you can buy a car — yes, a whole car — on Amazon. Same-day delivery not guaranteed. The e-commerce giant’s first foray into car shopping is called Amazon Auto. The company is partnering with Hyundai dealers in 48 cities in the US to list vehicles on the site. Customers can browse, order, find financing, and arrange delivery — all within the familiar confines of Amazon’s online ecosystem. Of course, if you’re looking for anything other than a Hyundai, you’re out of luck. At least for now. “With Amazon Autos, we’re bringing the simplicity and ease customers expect from Amazon to car shopping, one of their largest purchases, while offering dealers a new channel to connect with a broad audience,” Fan Jin, global head of Amazon Autos, said in a statement. “We’re excited to have Hyundai as our exclusive launch partner and look forward to welcoming more brands and expanding our selection to customers as the program grows.” Amazon first announced its plans to get into car buying last year, Previously, customers could browse car showrooms and compare prices on Amazon — but not actually buy a car. With the partnership with Hyundai, Amazon has finally added a key piece of the puzzle. And importantly, the end seller of the vehicle is still the dealer; Amazon’s platform will be the middleman between the customer and the dealership. As such, Amazon needs to appeal to dealers almost as much as it does to car shoppers. The company is making its pitch by arguing that it can offer “a new sales channel that connects them with millions of Amazon customers.” And with over 310 million active users, Amazon certainly has the numbers to back it up. Trade-ins will also be accepted through Amazon’s new car vertical. Customers will have to answer a series of questions about the conditions of the vehicle, after which the request will be processed by an “independent valuation service” to determine the value of the trade-in. [Image: A list of the 48 US cities where Amazon can sell you a car. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/25783460/Screenshot_2024_12_10_at_10.12.23_AM.png?quality=90&strip=all] And for a limited time, Amazon is sweetening the deal by offering a gift card for $2,300 for anyone who buys a car through the site. The card can be applied to the vehicle purchase, but the offer ends on January 10th, 2025. People typically hate car shopping, with most surveys showing that the dealership experience tops people’s lists of frustrations. Tesla has helped spearhead a movement toward a direct-to-consumer (DTC) model in which people buy their vehicles directly from the company, eschewing a dealership. Forty-eight states have laws that limit or ban manufacturers from selling vehicles directly to consumers — though that has started to shift recently thanks to Tesla’s popularity. Tesla has no independent dealerships, but dealership associations in multiple states have filed numerous lawsuits against Tesla to prevent the company from selling cars. Amazon’s deal with Hyundai neatly sidesteps this issue by ensuring that dealers remain a crucial part of the process. Most dealers allow customers to browse and buy a car through their own websites, but having Amazon as an additional platform with millions of daily customers is sure to help make the process even easier.

articles.title: Insta360’s new Ace Pro 2 has a bigger screen and AI-enhanced video recording.
articles.summary: Insta360’s new Ace Pro 2 features a larger, brighter screen, 8K video recording capabilities, and is powered by a pair of chips, improving its low-light recording capabilities.
articles.body_text: Insta360 has announced its new Ace Pro 2 action camera, an upgraded version of its GoPro Hero-series competitor. The compact camera now has a larger screen on the back that flips up 180 degrees for framing selfie videos, and it debuts at $399.99 — $50 cheaper than Insta360’s original Ace Pro. The design of the Ace Pro 2 still closely resembles the GoPro Hero series and DJI’s Osmo Action line, with an offset lens making room for an additional screen on the front. But while the front screen on the cameras of Insta360’s competitors can display full-color video, the Ace Pro 2’s monochromatic front screen only displays information. [Image: The front screen on the Ace Pro 2 is still limited to showing information, not video. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/25691858/insta360_2.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] That’s why the company is carrying forward the hinged screen from the original Ace Pro and has bumped its size from 2.42 inches to 2.5 inches (matching the screen size of the recently announced Osmo Action 5 Pro), while also improving its brightness and pixel density. A larger screen makes it easier to frame shots, whether you’re standing in front of or behind the camera. However, that hinge is also a durability risk depending on what you’re using the Ace Pro 2 for. The other feature that distinguishes Insta360’s new action cam from the competition is its 8K capabilities. The Ace Pro 2 can now record 8K video at 30fps — a slight bump from 8K at 24fps previously — using what Insta360 describes as a “next-gen” version of the 1/1.3-inch image sensor from the original Ace Pro that’s paired with a 157-degree wide-angle Leica Summarit lens. Still photography is also boosted to 50MP. Dropping the camera’s resolution down to 4K boosts frame rates to 120fps, or 60fps in HDR, while 1080p mode can record as high as 240fps for smooth slow-motion captures. Insta360 says the Ace Pro 2 is powered by a Pro Imaging Chip, handling “image processing and noise reduction,” as well as an AI chip running a “complex, custom-trained AI neural network,” powering a PureVideo recording mode. When recording at night or in places where the lighting is dim, the PureVideo mode can boost the brightness of a video while also enhancing details. The camera can also leverage its AI capabilities to automatically create edited clips featuring what it decides are the best moments in a video. [Image: An optional Dive Case accessory lets the Ace Pro 2 be used at depths of 197 feet. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/25691860/insta360_3.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] The Ace Pro 2’s waterproofing has been extended to 39 feet — six feet deeper than the original — or 197 feet when used with an optional Dive Case accessory. Insta360 has also added a new “wind guard” to the front of the camera to improve the quality of audio captured during high-speed activities but with a magnetic mount so it can be easily removed when recording in quieter situations. Other features include a larger 1,800mAh battery that Insta360 says is rated at 180 minutes but with video recording limited to 1080p at 24fps. In 8K mode, battery life will definitely be shorter than that. The Ace Pro 2 can also continually capture up to 120 seconds before a recording is started to reduce the chances of missing a shot, allows recordings to be paused without creating a new video file, and supports both hand gestures and voice commands for operating the camera from afar. What Insta360 didn’t announce today is an updated version of the Ace camera that debuted alongside the original Ace Pro. Its video capabilities were limited to 6K at 30fps, but it was $70 cheaper than the Pro. Had a new version of the Ace debuted with the same $50 price cut as the new Ace Pro 2, it would have potentially been a cheaper alternative to both the $349 Osmo Action 5 Pro and $399 GoPro Hero 13 Black while offering better video capture capabilities.

articles.title: The UK just laid out new rules for the internet — it only gets harder from here
articles.summary: Regulator Ofcom has published its first guidelines for how tech firms can comply with the UK’s Online Safety Act. They cover how platforms have to handle illegal content.
articles.body_text: After the Online Safety Act’s arduous multiyear passage through the UK’s lawmaking process, regulator Ofcom has published its first guidelines for how tech firms can comply with the mammoth legislation. Its proposal — part of a multiphase publication process — outlines how social media platforms, search engines, online and mobile games, and pornography sites should deal with illegal content like child sexual abuse material (CSAM), terrorism content, and fraud. Today’s guidelines are being released as proposals so Ofcom can gather feedback before the UK Parliament approves them toward the end of next year. Even then, the specifics will be voluntary. Tech firms can guarantee they’re obeying the law by following the guidelines to the letter, but they can take their own approach so long as they demonstrate compliance with the act’s overarching rules (and, presumably, are prepared to fight their case with Ofcom). “What this does for the first time is to put a duty of care on tech firms to have a responsibility for the safety of their users,” Ofcom’s online safety lead, Gill Whitehead, tells The Verge in an interview. “When they become aware that there is illegal content on their platform, they have got to get it down, and they also need to conduct risk assessments to understand the specific risks that those services might carry.” The aim is to require that sites be proactive to stop the spread of illegal content and not just play whack-a-mole after the fact. It’s meant to encourage a switch from a reactive to a more proactive approach, says lawyer Claire Wiseman, who specializes in tech, media, telecoms, and data. Ofcom estimates that around 100,000 services may fall under the wide-ranging rules, though only the largest and highest-risk platforms will have to abide by the strictest requirements. Ofcom recommends these platforms implement policies like not allowing strangers to send direct messages to children, using hash matching to detect and remove CSAM, maintaining content and search moderation teams, and offering ways for users to report harmful content. Large tech platforms already follow many of these practices, but Ofcom hopes to see them implemented more consistently. “We think they represent best practice of what’s out there, but it’s not necessarily applied across the board,” Whitehead says. “Some firms are applying it sporadically but not necessarily systematically, and so we think there is a great benefit for a more wholesale, widespread adoption.” There’s also one big outlier: the platform known as X (formerly Twitter). The UK’s efforts with the legislation long predate Elon Musk’s acquisition of Twitter, but it was passed as he fired large swaths of its trust and safety teams and presided over a loosening of moderation standards, which could put X at odds with regulators. Ofcom’s guidelines, for example, specify that users should be able to easily block users — but Musk has publicly stated his intentions to remove X’s block feature. He’s clashed with the EU over similar rules and reportedly even considered pulling out of the European market to avoid them. Whitehead declined to comment when I asked whether X had been cooperative in talks with Ofcom but said the regulator had been “broadly encouraged” by the response from tech firms generally. Ofcom’s regulations also cover how sites should deal with other illegal harms like content that encourages or assists suicide or serious self-harm, harassment, revenge porn and other sexual exploitation, and the supply of drugs and firearms. Search services should provide “crisis prevention information” when users enter suicide-related queries, for example, and when companies update their recommendation algorithms, they should conduct risk assessments to check that they’re not going to amplify illegal content. If users suspect that a site isn’t complying with the rules, Whitehead says there’ll be a route to complain directly to Ofcom. If a firm is found to be in breach, Ofcom can levy fines of up to £18 million (around $22 million) or 10 percent of worldwide turnover — whichever is higher. Offending sites can even be blocked in the UK. Today’s consultation covers some of the Online Safety Act’s least contentious territory, like reducing the spread of content that was already illegal in the UK. As Ofcom releases future updates, it will have to take on touchier subjects, like content that’s legal but harmful for children, underage access to pornography, and protections for women and girls. Perhaps most controversially, it will need to interpret a section that critics have claimed could fundamentally undermine end-to-end encryption in messaging apps. The section in question allows Ofcom to require online platforms to use so-called “accredited technology” to detect CSAM. But WhatsApp, other encrypted messaging services, and digital rights groups say this scanning would require breaking apps’ encryption systems and invading user privacy. Whitehead says that Ofcom plans to consult on this next year, leaving its full impact on encrypted messaging uncertain. There’s another technology not emphasized in today’s consultation: artificial intelligence. But that doesn’t mean AI-generated content won’t fall under the rules. The Online Safety Act attempts to address online harms in a “technology neutral” way, Whitehead says, regardless of how they’ve been created. So AI-generated CSAM would be in scope by virtue of it being CSAM, and a deepfake used to conduct fraud would be in scope by virtue of the fraud. “We’re not regulating the technology, we’re regulating the context,” Whitehead says. While Ofcom says it’s trying to take a collaborative, proportionate approach to the Online Safety Act, its rules could still prove onerous for sites that aren’t tech juggernauts. BBC News notes that Ofcom’s initial set of guidance is over 1,500 pages long. The Wikimedia Foundation, the nonprofit behind Wikipedia, tells The Verge that it’s proving increasingly challenging to comply with different regulatory regimes across the world, even if it supports the idea of regulation in general. “We are already struggling with our capacity to comply with the [EU’s] Digital Services Act,” the Wikimedia Foundation’s VP for global advocacy, Rebecca MacKinnon, says, pointing out that the nonprofit has just a handful of lawyers dedicated to the EU regulations compared to the legions that companies like Meta and Google can dedicate. “We agree as a platform that we have responsibilities,” MacKinnon says, but “when you’re a nonprofit and every hour of work is zero sum, that’s problematic.” Ofcom’s Whitehead admits that the Online Safety Act and Digital Services Act are more “regulatory cousins” than “identical twins,” which means complying with both takes extra work. She says Ofcom is trying to make operating across different countries easier, pointing toward the regulator’s work setting up a global online safety regulator network. Passing the Online Safety Act during a turbulent era in British politics was already difficult. But as Ofcom begins filling in its details, the real challenges may be only beginning. Update November 9th, 3:04AM ET: Updated to note guidance is over 1,500 pages long.

articles.title: On the cusp of 24/7 service, robotaxis face pleas and protest in San Francisco
articles.summary: Waymo and Cruise are poised to expand robotaxi service in San Francisco to 24/7 operation. But city officials are concerned about blocked traffic, and some residents are using orange cones in protest.
articles.body_text: On a recent Friday evening, a driverless car pulled up alongside an outdoor dining shed in the Mission district of San Francisco, put on its hazard lights, and waited. As traffic began to pile up behind the vehicle, a man smoking a cigarette outside a nearby bar rolled his eyes. “I don’t drive a car,” he grumbled, “so I don’t really care about these things.” Other residents of this hilly city by the bay are not so ambivalent about the coming onslaught of autonomous cars. The California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) is poised to vote this Thursday on whether to allow Cruise and Waymo, the two main companies with autonomous vehicles in San Francisco, to expand their paid ridehailing services to operate 24/7. Currently, the companies only offer limited service. A vote in favor of the companies would essentially give robotaxis full access to the peninsula and its residents. They would be able to operate similarly to Uber or Lyft — travel anywhere in the city, at any time of day, and charge money for the rides. The vote also represents “the most significant regulatory moment for autonomous vehicles in the US over the last/next 3 years,” said Reilly Brennan, general partner at venture capital firm Trucks. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/24780669/1497019989.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] According to Brennan, a robotaxi’s service area is also its total addressable market, a term in corporate finance that usually describes how much possible revenue a company can make. “If CPUC says it cannot operate 24 hours per day, you effectively have a reduced total addressable market,” he said in an email. “That’s why this upcoming vote is so critical: we’ll find out if the most significant US state (by revenue) is giving a green, yellow or red light to AV robotaxi’s future.” City officials are praying for a red light, or at least a yellow one. For months, they have been pleading with the state to delay the vote, citing a spate of incidents in which autonomous vehicles have stopped traffic, blocked buses, or obstructed emergency vehicles. The city’s transit agency and fire and police department have all logged complaints with the CPUC, calling for the commission to reconsider the plan for 24/7 service. “They’re not ready for prime time,” San Francisco Fire Chief Jeanine Nicholson told the Los Angeles Times recently. The department has logged 66 incidents since May 2022 in which robotaxis have interfered with firetrucks, according to The Washington Post. Many incidents have gone viral: robotaxis blocking intersections, forcing bus passengers to get out and walk, driving over fire hoses. In May, body camera footage captured a cop wielding a road flare at a Cruise vehicle, barking at it to “stay” as if it were an unruly puppy. After a mass shooting in June that wounded nine people, a robotaxi blocked a lane of traffic in the Mission district, slowing down emergency vehicles. The state’s Department of Motor Vehicles has logged nearly 75 collisions involving autonomous vehicles this year, including one last May in which a Waymo vehicle ran over and killed a small dog. The vehicle was operating with a safety driver in the front seat. The companies have defended themselves, noting that they are in communication with city officials about ways to improve to avoid future incidents. They also note that no one has been seriously hurt or killed by an autonomous vehicle in San Francisco, while many people are killed every year by human-driven ones. Pedestrian deaths in the city, much like in the rest of the country, have ticked up each year. There were 20 pedestrians killed by drivers in 2017 and 39 in 2022, according to city data. But some residents aren’t taking the slow advance of robotaxi coverage lying down. An activist group calling itself Safe Street Rebel put out a call on social media for people to place orange traffic cones on the hoods of any robotaxi seen wandering the streets of San Francisco, which would effectively disable it. “Cruise & Waymo promise they’ll reduce traffic & collisions, but we know that’s not true,” the pseudonymous account wrote on Twitter last week. “They block busses & emergency vehicles, create more traffic, and are a surveillance nightmare.” [Media: https://twitter.com/SafeStreetRebel/status/1676695665278337024] Autonomous vehicles usually have more cameras on them than typical passenger vehicles. Police could request footage from those cameras to investigate crimes or to violate residents’ privacy, advocates say. Waymo has received some requests for camera footage from law enforcement agencies but says it generally requires a warrant or court order. The companies were quick to condemn the orange cone protest, with a Waymo spokesperson calling it “vandalism.” An unnamed Safe Street Rebel told us in a Twitter direct message that some of the AV companies have “threatened to call the cops on us.” And the San Francisco transit agency spoke out against “ANY actions that may increase the number of disabled AVs on San Francisco streets.” The spread of robotaxis is testing San Francisco’s desire to continue to play guinea pig to Silicon Valley’s futuristic experiments. “I do believe people are both fed up with heavily distracted human-piloted vehicles / driver distractions *and* also that there has been a public backlash against AV fleets in some cities,” Brennan said. “There is a public chorus for a better, safer experience in cities.” Update July 11 9:40AM ET: Updated to include reactions to the orange cone protest.

articles.title: White House announces 25 percent tariff on Chinese tech goods
articles.summary: Today, President Trump announced an aggressive new set of tariffs against China, specifically naming touchscreens, batteries, and electric motors. Experts fear the move may provoke a trade war.
articles.body_text: Today, President Trump announced an aggressive new set of tariffs against China, setting a 25 percent import tax on $50 billion worth of “industrially significant technologies” imported from China. In previous discussions, China has threatened to retaliate against such tariffs, stoking fears of a far-reaching and unpredictable trade war between the countries. US Customs and Border Protection is set to begin collecting the tariffs on July 6th. A list published by the White House details more than 1,000 specific products that will be affected by the tariffs. It includes a broad range of components used in electronics manufacturing, specifically naming touchscreens, batteries, and electric motors. General components like transistors are also named on the list as well as more specific components used in televisions, cameras, and radio receivers. Fiber optic cables are also on the list, although most fiber optic cable is manufactured by US companies. Notably, the list does not include cellphones or completed televisions. Today’s list is a revision of an earlier proposal that was published in April that removed 515 items and proposed an additional 284. According to the White House, the tariffs are targeted at China’s “Made in China 2025” initiative, which aims to promote high-tech manufacturing within the country. “The United States can no longer tolerate losing our technology and intellectual property through unfair economic practices,” the White House said in a statement. In a response issued last night, China’s ministry of commerce pledged to respond with tariffs of “the same scale and the same strength.” The White House statement also pledged to implement additional tariffs if China retaliated, sparking fears of an escalating trade war that could significantly limit trade between the two countries.

Steven Spielberg’s Ready Player One improves immensely on the book
articles.summary: Ernest Cline’s fast-moving, bestselling novel was a treasure trove for pop-culture junkies. But the endless references to video games and movies work better on the screen, where most of them originated in the first place.
articles.body_text: Fans tend to either love or hate Ernest Cline’s bestselling 2011 novel Ready Player One. There are legitimate reasons for both reactions. On the love side: it’s a light, airy pop confection, crammed with familiar cultural references, which Cline recontextualizes in surprising ways. On the hate side: the prose can be extremely clumsy, as it is in this paragraph where teenage protagonist Wade Watts describes the virtual car he constructed for himself in the vast online world where he spends most of his waking hours: > The DeLorean came outfitted with a (nonfunctioning) flux capacitor, but I’d made several additions to its equipment and appearance. First, I’d installed an artificially intelligent onboard computer named KITT (purchased in an online auction) into the dashboard, along with a matching red Knight Rider scanner just above the DeLorean’s grill. Then I’d outfitted the car with an oscillation overthruster, a device that allowed it to travel through solid matter. Finally, to complete my ‘80s super-vehicle theme, I’d slapped a Ghostbusters logo on each of the DeLorean’s gull-wing doors, then added personalized plates that read ECTO-88. That’s a lot of awkward verbiage to say two pretty basic things: people in virtual reality can express their personal tastes through their avatars in hyper-specific ways, and Cline is so obsessed with the culture of the 1980s — the geek-fodder of his youth — that he thinks it’s compelling even in the form of a shopping list. The book is a fast-paced adventure, but this kind of unwieldy lump of mix-and-match nostalgia acts as a roadblock. There’s no attempt to consider why Wade finds these specific objects appealing, out of the billion options available to him. The book assumes up front that readers find everything in this list as unbearably cool as Cline does, and that just running down an exhaustive list of Wade’s favorite things is enough to make him appealing, relatable, and enviable. Steven Spielberg’s new film adaptation of Ready Player One prominently features that same car, but in a context that improves it immensely. Spielberg doesn’t have Wade talk audiences through it, and he doesn’t spell out the references. He just slaps the car down in the middle of a tremendous early action scene, where it’s prominent, distinctive, and memorable. Fans who want the full nostalgia trip, who want to wring every Easter egg out of the experience, will eventually be able to pause the movie and frame-by-frame through it, looking for the flux capacitor on the dashboard, checking the plates, and scanning for extra bonus material. But in the middle of the action, even to people who’ve never seen the Back to the Future movies and aren’t vibing on the connection, the car doesn’t need explaining. It’s just a sleek piece of visual energy, one breathless element among dozens of others. It’s not a citation or a list. It’s an effortless, integrated piece of the action. [Media: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cSp1dM2Vj48] That dynamic stretches throughout Ready Player One, scripted by Cline and X-Men: The Last Stand writer Zak Penn, and directed by Spielberg as a whiplash-fast tear through a world-spanning, all-encompassing video game. The story, which mostly takes place in the virtual-reality world called The OASIS, rarely slows down enough to explain the references, or geek out over them the way the book does. It’s still a visual festival of ‘80s culture that sometimes hinges significant jokes on the assumption that the audience knows the filmography of Robert Zemeckis, or will chortle over a reference to Monty Python and the Holy Grail. But the film improves significantly on the book by prioritizing the story over the signifiers. The hardcore pop-culture crowd that is this movie’s ultimate intended audience will have plenty to pore over and pick apart in this film. But the story moves briskly enough, and with enough giant-sized, screen-friendly excitement, that it doesn’t feel like it’s aimed solely and specifically at them. Some of that speed comes at the expense of artistry. Ready Player One opens by laboriously climbing a mountain of voiceover, explaining the setting: the year is 2045, and the world is terrible. Most people live in depressing poverty, and spend as much time as possible jacked into the fantasy world of the OASIS. There, they can be and do anything they want, or at least anything they can afford to buy with coins won in the universe’s eternally running video game arenas. The OASIS was created by reclusive genius James Halliday (Bridge of Spies’ Mark Rylance), who packed it with his own favorite culture. When he died, he created a three-part quest within the world, linked to his favorite films and games, but also tied to his own past regrets and frustrations. Whoever finds the three keys he’s hidden within the game world, and the ultimate Easter egg they unlock, will get full control of OASIS and Halliday’s vast fortune. The quest has created a subclass of “egg-hunters,” or “Gunters” — quest-obsessives whose full-time occupation is hunting down the keys. It’s also created an evil dystopian megacorp, run by former Halliday intern Nolan Sorrento (Ben Mendelsohn, of Rogue One and Starred Up), and devoted to gaining control of the OASIS to commercialize it. Wade (X-Men: Apocalypse’s Tye Sheridan) and his fellow Gunters — particularly too-cool-for-school solo hunter Art3mis (Olivia Cooke, also currently starring in the chilling Thoroughbreds) and Wade’s big mechanical buddy Aech (Master of None’s Lena Waithe) — all want the keys and the egg for their own personal reasons, though those are barely articulated. Cline’s book assumes everyone will know a DeLorean is cool; Spielberg’s film assumes the same thing about a teenage protagonist who loves playing video games. Wade (or Parzival, as he’s known in the OASIS) eventually develops an ethos, but for the most part, he’s like every other video gamer who’s ever sat down on a couch and hit “start” on the controller. He may appreciate the gameplay or the storyline or the people he meets online, but ultimately, he just wants that elusive win. He’s more a customized audience avatar than a real character, but that’s fitting for a world that’s so spottily drawn, at least outside of the virtual paradise where people prefer to spent their time. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/9820163/29ed3d416cd513893ea80d1e6c9a560e.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] The film version of Ready Player One has some major advantages over the book. The exposition is just as bald, but once it’s done, Spielberg can focus on the endless dynamism of a world where anything is possible. As Wade and others follow their quest through races, battles, and puzzles, they encounter a dizzying blur of visual references that act as “Hey, remember this?” in-jokes with the audience, including some major ones that weren’t in the book. But the filmmakers also delve into Halliday’s past and his wounded psyche, in a way that gradually becomes a little touching and tragic. (A conversation with Halliday’s online avatar closely recalls a similar scene with Professor Falken in WarGames, and carries the same sense of melancholy.) The film also goes further than the book in laying out why Halliday’s retreat into a fantasy world wasn’t necessarily good for anyone — especially not for Halliday himself. No matter how validating the onscreen gags are, they’re still a reminder of a man who found more emotional resonance in Jurassic Park’s T-Rex than in a connection with a living human being. The film inevitably has its cake and eats it too when it comes to addressing wish-fulfillment fantasy and delirious nostalgia: the story can only push so far in sorrowing over Halliday’s surrender and retreat from the world, while still turning every rambunctious game setpiece into a celebration of Cline’s favorite culture. Ready Player One is so heavily inspired by and inflected with the broad, black-and-white morality of ‘80s geek culture that any attempt to find the gray areas feels slightly daring, even as it feels slightly out of place. Given that Sorrento is a buttoned-down, stony-faced idea-thief of an evil overlord, straight out of Tron, there’s not a lot of room for narrative nuance in this story. But at least Cline and Penn make the effort, acknowledging some of the biggest complaints leveled at Cline’s book, and trying to take the story a little deeper. The film version does carry over some of the book’s most notable flaws, especially a suspicious reliance on narrative convenience and coincidence. The characters are thinly drawn, and most of them are little more than cool avatars and signature moves. There’s no sense that anyone involved with the story really cares about the details of the real world in this crapsack future, given how little the real-world scenes hold together. And the film takes a particularly feather-light approach to what should be significant emotions, especially when a death that should devastate Wade is shrugged off within seconds, then brought back out for a cheap, unearned moment much later. Spielberg’s signature sentiment is operating in full force, as he builds up one highly symbolic confrontation solely for the feelings of triumph and justice it creates, and then has it come to exactly nothing. And in places, the story jumps forward so quickly that it feels like necessary connective scenes are simply missing. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/10408527/ready_player_one.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Unequivocally, the film’s biggest problem is the half-assed love story between Wade and Art3mis, which operates on approximately 75 percent wish-fulfillment and 25 percent apathetic inevitability. When they first encounter each other, Wade is starstruck: he knows Art3mis from her online cool-girl rep, and watching her in action, he sees her as an über-badass with leet skillz and an appealingly punk devil-may-care attitude. It’s a short, shocking jump from there to him telling her he loves her. What follows should be important and telling — she reminds him that they don’t know each other, that he’s seeing an online avatar and a mental picture he’s largely invented. (And, of course, he thinks they’re perfect for each other because she gets his references.) But the film never follows through on that mature and useful point. The insta-relationship that develops between them is as inauthentic and insulting as the central romance in Edgar Wright’s Scott Pilgrim Vs. The World, without any of the sense of irony or intentionality. It’s bad enough to follow the “hero wins the girl as a prize” model without examining it at all. It’s worse still to have the characters examine it, find the flaws, then instantly forget about them. This isn’t a movie with a long memory (except when it’s reaching back 40 years for visual gags), but it’s infuriating to see it try to examine its own tropes responsibly, then take no steps whatsoever to address the issues it raises. And yet, when Wade is in his kitted-out DeLorean, tearing along a preposterously difficult game racetrack, menaced by King Kong and dodging flying debris as his fellow racers crash and burn, very little of that matters. The sheer dynamism and energy of the movie are compelling, even when the character drama isn’t. The action scenes are deliberately overclocked and overwhelming, turning Wade’s quest into a thrilling blur of fast-paced decisions and the endorphin-rush highs of a good gaming experience. More importantly, the film is overtly funny in ways that constantly remind the audience that there are people behind the game avatars, and specifically people who are sometimes young, self-absorbed, immature, and caught up in their own created self-images of badassery. The human frailties behind the game avatars is a reliable well of humor for Ready Player One, and the script takes full, hilarious advantage. And while the film’s real world gets left behind in the rush, the attention to detail during the OASIS scenes is absolutely astounding — not just the details Cline salivated over on the page, like that Knight Rider scanner in the grill of Wade’s car, but the subtle nuances, like the way Wade’s avatar constantly seems to be standing in a flattering breeze that ruffles his hair in the most winsome way possible, or the way Art3mis’ too-big anime eyes catch the light. The uncanny-valley effect is strong in these game avatars, but Spielberg uses it to his advantage, reminding his audience at every moment that what they’re seeing is mostly a fantasy, created by people who see image as almost everything. It’s a slick, sleek, surface fantasy, for sure. But for people who share Cline’s worldview, or identify with gamer culture in general, it’s an immense hit of validation and acknowledgement, delivered with joyful abandon and unmissable enthusiasm. All those feelings of love and obsession came through clearly on the page. But on the screen, they’re bigger and better, because they’re so much more intense, and so much closer to the memorable images that turned Cline into an obsessive in the first place. This review was initially published after Ready Player One’s premiere at the 2018 SXSW festival in Austin, Texas. The film arrives in theaters on March 29th, 2018.

articles.summary: En 34-årig kvinna och en 48-årig man döms för att ha våldtagit och misshandlat en man med en kötthammare.
articles.body_text: En 34-årig kvinna och en 48-årig man döms för att ha våldtagit och misshandlat en man med en kötthammare. Tingsrätten anser att de handlat med ”särskild hänsynslöshet och råhet” och dömer dem till sex års fängelse. Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Händelsen inträffade för två år sedan hemma hos målsäganden, en man i 55-årsåldern, i Stockholm . Han har berättat att de tre festade hemma hos kvinnan, som är hans granne. Han blev anklagad för att ha ”kladdat” på henne, vilket enligt honom inte stämde. De gick hem till honom, där han utsattes för en grov och utdragen misshandel. Kvinnan och mannen slog honom med en kötthammare i huvudet, i ansiktet och på kroppen, tryckte ner hans huvud i ett vattenfyllt badkar och stack en kniv i hans armar och ben. De våldtog honom också med kötthammarens skaft. Efteråt har han haft panikattacker och mardrömmar om att han är under vatten. 48-åringen förnekar brott. Han har sagt att han slog målsäganden när denne, enligt honom, antastat kvinnan, att målsäganden ramlade i trappan på väg hem till sig och därefter misshandlades i sin lägenhet av tre andra män, som han inte vill namnge. Kvinnan har uppgett att hon slog målsäganden i ansiktet i nödvärn när han utsatte henne för vad hon beskriver som ett våldtäktsförsök. Hon har förnekat allt våld i övrigt och säger sig inte veta hur han fick sina skador. Även hon har sagt att ytterligare tre män fanns på platsen. Efterhandskonstruktioner, anser tingsrätten, och konstaterar att målsägandens berättelse stöds av omfattande bevisning: Hans skador är förenliga med det våld han beskrivit.

Medan V-ledaren framhåller partiets kompromissvilja anklagar S-ledaren V för att ha vägrat förhandla. Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Läget ser tufft ut för de rödgröna partierna sedan V i söndags tackade nej till budet från S, C och MP. I stället har C vänt sig högerut och återupptagit samtalen med M, KD och L. På måndag ska riksdagen rösta om Ulf Kristersson (M) som statsminister. Nu har V-ledaren Nooshi Dadgostar skrivit ett internt brev till partimedlemmarna där hon redogör för de havererade förhandlingarna. ” Jag förstår alla som undrar om vi kunde gjort något annorlunda, men i grund och botten handlar det om att Centerpartiets ledning hela tiden har velat gå högerut ”, skriver hon i brevet, som Expressen har tagit del av. Dadgostar framhåller att partiet har deltagit i alla möten och förhandlingar som det bjudits in till, lagt fram egna förslag och undersökt möjligheterna till kompromisser för att lösa upp knutarna. ” Det bud som presenterades i Expressen i söndags var så långt som Centerpartiet ville sträcka sig. Det innebar vissa förbättringar, men inte någon avgörande ny politisk inriktning för Sverige ”, skriver V-ledaren. Men S-ledaren Magdalena Andersson ger en helt annan bild av förhandlingarna. I ett internt brev till de socialdemokratiska partimedlemmarna, som Expressen också har tagit del av, skriver hon att Vänsterpartiet inte har velat delta i några förhandlingar överhuvudtaget.

articles.title: Nya Brattåsmannens offer berättar: ”Jag var rädd”
articles.summary: Mannen är lik fantombilden – har varken hörts eller topsats i utredningen
articles.body_text: En man med noll impulskontroll, missbruksproblematik och dessutom ett våldskapital enligt polisen. Mannen som nu dragits in i Brattåsutredningen har varken hörts i utredningen eller topsats – och nu är han död, enligt Expressens uppgifter. – Jag var rädd för hans gränslösa beteende, säger ett av hans tidigare offer. Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Ångermanlands tingsrätt dömde i höstas Johan Jacobsson, 45, till 14 års fängelse för medhjälp till dubbelmordet i Brattås . Domen överklagades och utvecklingen inför den hovrättsförhandling som startade tidigare under onsdagen har varit dramatisk. Åklagare Hanna Flordal har visserligen hela tiden lämnat fältet öppet för att det kan finnas flera gärningspersoner och eftersom Johan Jacobsson dömdes för medhjälp till mord har även tingsrätten konstaterat att en mördare går fri. Men i elfte timmen har ny DNA-bevisning lämnats in, vilket SVT har avslöjat. Den pekar mot en man som aldrig varit aktuell i utredningen tidigare. Detta trots att mannen fram till sin död för ett par år sedan bodde hela sitt liv i området och var välkänd av polisen, enligt Expressens uppgifter. DNA-spåret från mannen har hittats på en fårfäll som dolde Tor Öbergs döda kropp där den låg i en lada på hans gård. Det skedde ett inbrott på gården efter mordet där maskiner stals, men det har inte framkommit om det har varit möjligt att datera spåret från mannen till före eller efter mordet, när fällen låg orörd kvar i ladan innan polisen beslagtog den. Så här beskriver den nya Brattåsmannen sig själv i ett polisförhör: Svår ADHD, låg impulskontroll och lågt konsekvenstänk. Medicineras för detta vilket inte är helt okomplicerat. Har svårt att sortera och koncentrera sig när flertalet intryck kommer samtidigt. Mannen – som var i 60-årsåldern vid sin bortgång – sätter en kritiserad fantombild som använts i utredningen i ett nytt ljus. Fantombilden från 2009 baserades på ett vittne som sa sig ha sett en man med ett ”härjat utseende” nära brottsplatsen och föreställde en medelålders man i 45–50-årsåldern. Den medhjälpsdömde Johan Jakobsson var i 25-årsåldern vid tiden för dådet. Men den nu avlidna mannen var vid tiden för mordet nära det åldersspannet och hade ett härjat utseende efter många års narkotikamissbruk.

articles.title: Dåligt väder – svensk stridspilot kunde inte skjuta ner rysk robot
articles.summary: Två misstänkta ryska robotar och en jetdriven drönare tog sig in i polskt luftrum. En svensk stridspilot i en Jas 39 Gripen under Natobefäl fick tillstånd att skjuta ner en robot – men kunde inte, skriver Kyiv Independent. En svensk stridspilot i en Jas 39 Gripen under Natobefäl fick tillstånd att skjuta ner en robot – men kunde inte, skriver Kyiv Independent. – Det var väldigt svåra förhållanden och våra piloter visade upp en stark handlingskraft, säger Hanna Heurlin på Försvarsmakten till TV4 . Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. I samband med en omfattande rysk attack mot Ukraina den 20 november tog sig tre luftburna objekt, två misstänkta robotar och en jetdriven drönare, in i polskt luftrum. Kyiv Independent rapporterar att två svenska Jas Gripen-plan och två polska F-16-plan sattes in, med stöd av ett radarspaningsplan av typen Saab 340 och ett nederländskt lufttankningsplan. Enligt generallöjtnant Ireneusz Nowak fick en svensk stridspilot tillstånd att skjuta ner en misstänkt rysk kryssningsrobot av typen Ch-101, skriver tidningen. Dåligt väder ska dock ha gjort att piloten inte kunde identifiera målet ordentligt, varken visuellt eller med planets elektrooptiska sensorer. Därför öppnade han inte eld. De svenska Jas Gripen-planen opererade under Nato-ledning och hade alltså fått tillstånd att bekämpa fientliga mål om identifieringskraven var uppfyllda. Enligt Polens regering slog de ryska robotarna och drönaren ner på polskt territorium. Ingen person ska ha kommit till skada. Hanna Heurlin, vakthavande kommunikatör på Försvarsmakten, sa under helgen till TV4 att hon inte kunde kommentera vad det var för föremål som Gripenplanet försökte genskjuta. – Det var väldigt svåra förhållanden och våra piloter visade upp stark handlingskraft och detta påvisar även vikten av att vi deltar i Natos kollektiva försvar, säger hon till kanalen.

articles.body_text: Eller bli ett konstruktivt oppositionsparti? C-toppen Effie Kourlos öppnar för att partiet kan släppa fram en borgerlig trepartiregering. – Det tror jag har goda chanser att ena C, som en kompromiss. Men det är inte det som är på bordet nu, säger statsvetaren Andreas Johansson Heinö. Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Moderaternas ledare Ulf Kristersson vill bilda en borgerlig fyrpartiregering och på måndag ska riksdagen rösta om honom som statsminister. Sverigedemokraternas ledare Jimmie Åkesson har sagt att man kommer att släppa fram en sådan regering och sedan gå i opposition. Avgörandet ligger hos Centerpartiet – som är djupt splittrat i frågan. Hinner partiet landa i en lösning? Andreas Johansson Heinö, statsvetare och förläggare på Timbro, är tveksam. – Röstar man nej på måndag, då finns det bara en statsministervotering kvar och alternativet är extra val. Då har C en dålig förhandlingsposition, eftersom de skulle ha väldigt dåliga förutsättningar i ett extra val. Den rationella analysen är att C har minst att förlora på att släppa fram Kristerssons regeringsalternativ, men partier är inte alltid rationella. Om det är väldigt känsligt för C att sitta med i en borgerlig regering som är beroende av SD:s stöd, skulle de kunna släppa fram och samarbeta med en borgerlig trepartiregering? – Det tror jag har goda chanser att ena C, som en kompromiss. Men det är inte det som är på bordet nu. Kristersson fick frågan på en pressträff och sa: ”Det är inget alternativ som jag har övervägt.” Vi vet inte hur SD skulle agera heller, säger Andreas Johansson Heinö och fortsätter: – Det finns en poäng för Jimmie Åkesson i att koppla ihop C med de gamla allianspartierna. Det är inte givet alls att SD skulle släppa fram en borgerlig trepartiregering.
